items.explanation: Progressives cleaned up city government, workplaces, and the tax code — but farm laborers, especially migrants, saw little of this reform energy.
options: A. City governments like Cleveland's became more efficient
B. Factory health and safety improved in places
C. Conditions for migrant farm workers markedly improved
D. A national income tax was established
items.stem: Progressive reforms achieved all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Cleveland under Tom Johnson really did become a model of efficient, reform-minded city government — this was a genuine Progressive achievement, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Factory health and safety really did improve in places — through state laws on hours, child labor, and workplace conditions. This was real Progressive progress, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. Progressive reform energy largely bypassed migrant farm workers, who remained outside the era's labor protections and reform campaigns.
option_explanations.D: A national income tax really was established — the Sixteenth Amendment (1913) authorized it. This was a genuine Progressive achievement, not the exception.

items.explanation: Roosevelt was furious when Taft's Justice Department moved against U.S. Steel — a trust Roosevelt himself had approved — convincing him Taft had betrayed progressivism and driving the 1912 Bull Moose bolt.
options: A. Taft's administration was uniformly anti-progressive
B. He wanted to split the GOP and elect a Democrat
C. He was outraged by the Ballinger-Pinchot affair
D. Taft moved against U.S. Steel under the Sherman Act
items.stem: Theodore Roosevelt ran for president in 1912 because

option_explanations.A: Taft was not uniformly anti-progressive — he filed more antitrust suits than Roosevelt and supported some reforms. 'Uniformly anti-progressive' overstates the break, and it was not what drove Roosevelt to run.
option_explanations.B: Roosevelt did not run to split the GOP and elect a Democrat, though that is what happened (Wilson won). His motive was personal and political fury at Taft, not a scheme to hand the election to the Democrats.
option_explanations.C: The Ballinger-Pinchot affair angered Roosevelt, but it was an earlier, secondary grievance. What drove him to run in 1912 was the U.S. Steel suit — a trust he had personally approved — which convinced him Taft had betrayed progressivism.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Roosevelt was furious when Taft's Justice Department moved against U.S. Steel under the Sherman Act — a combination Roosevelt himself had blessed in 1907. To Roosevelt this proved Taft had turned against the progressive program, and it drove the 1912 Bull Moose bolt.

items.explanation: Wilson's era was a nadir: Birth of a Nation glorified the Klan, Black-Progressive alliances never formed, and Washington's access to Roosevelt faded — all true, all discouraging.
options: A. Birth of a Nation smeared Black Reconstruction
B. Black and Progressive leaders failed to ally
C. Washington's influence with Roosevelt waned
D. All of the above
items.stem: Black Americans found the Wilson years discouraging because

option_explanations.A: Birth of a Nation (1915) really did smear Black Reconstruction — glorifying the Klan and portraying Black officeholders as corrupt. This was genuinely discouraging, but it is only one of three true causes.
option_explanations.B: Black and Progressive leaders really did fail to ally — most white Progressives ignored or opposed Black civil rights. This was genuinely discouraging, but only one of three true causes.
option_explanations.C: Booker T. Washington's influence with Theodore Roosevelt really did wane — and Roosevelt was out of office by 1913 anyway. This was genuinely discouraging, but only one of three true causes.
option_explanations.D: Correct — all three are true and all three made the Wilson years discouraging for Black Americans: Birth of a Nation's glorification of the Klan, the failure of Black and Progressive leaders to ally, and the fading of Washington's White House access.

items.explanation: Both camps agreed industrial capitalism had produced obscene inequality — but Progressives wanted to regulate it while Socialists wanted to replace it.
options: A. Capitalism had created vast inequality
B. The factory system must be fundamentally rebuilt
C. Labor unions were inherently evil
D. Revolution was the only remedy

option_explanations.A: Correct. Both camps agreed that industrial capitalism had produced vast, obscene inequality — they split on the remedy: Progressives wanted to regulate capitalism, Socialists wanted to replace it. The agreement was on the diagnosis.
option_explanations.B: Progressives did not want to rebuild the factory system fundamentally — they wanted to regulate and reform it (safety laws, antitrust). Only the Socialists wanted a fundamental rebuilding.
option_explanations.C: Neither camp thought labor unions were inherently evil — both supported organized labor. Hostility to unions was a business position, not a Progressive or Socialist one.
option_explanations.D: Only the Socialists saw revolution as the remedy. Progressives explicitly rejected revolution in favor of reform through law and regulation.

items.explanation: Social Gospel ministers, Debs followers, and Bull Moosers all marched under the progressive banner — a U.S. Steel magnate, whose trust the Progressives meant to tame, did not.
options: A. A Social Gospel minister
B. A major U.S. Steel stockholder
C. A follower of Eugene Debs
D. A Bull Moose Party member
items.stem: Who was LEAST likely to be a Progressive in this era?

option_explanations.A: Social Gospel ministers were very likely Progressives — the Social Gospel taught that Christians must reform society's ills, making ministers natural reformers.
option_explanations.B: Correct. A major U.S. Steel stockholder was the least likely Progressive — U.S. Steel was exactly the kind of giant trust the Progressives meant to tame, and its owners had every interest in resisting regulation.
option_explanations.C: A follower of Eugene Debs was likely a Progressive-adjacent reformer — Debs's Socialists shared the Progressives' diagnosis of inequality, even while differing on the cure.
option_explanations.D: A Bull Moose Party member was by definition a Progressive — the 1912 Bull Moose (Progressive) Party was Roosevelt's reform vehicle.

items.explanation: The act plants federal inspectors inside the plants -- 'access at all times, by day or night' -- and gives their judgment the force of a government stamp: 'Inspected and passed.' The mechanism is continuous federal presence plus an official seal, not voluntary codes, state action, or prohibition of the industry.
options: A. Voluntary self-regulation by the packing companies
B. Continuous federal presence inside plants plus a government stamp of approval
C. Inspections conducted by the state governments
D. An outright ban on industrial meatpacking
items.stem: The inspection system described in the act relied on
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the purposes hereinbefore set forth the Secretary shall cause to be made, by inspectors appointed for that purpose, an examination and inspection of all cattle, sheep, swine, and goats before they shall be allowed to enter into any slaughtering, packing, or canning establishment..."
—Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The opposite of the act's approach. The 1906 law did not trust packing companies to regulate themselves — it imposed mandatory federal inspection precisely because voluntary practices had failed.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The act plants federal inspectors inside the plants — with 'access at all times, by day or night' — and gives their judgment the force of a government stamp: 'Inspected and passed.' The mechanism is continuous federal presence plus an official seal.
option_explanations.C: The inspection system was federal, not state. The act created federal inspectors appointed under the Secretary of Agriculture — a national system, not fifty state ones.
option_explanations.D: The act did not ban industrial meatpacking — it regulated it. Packing continued; it now operated under federal inspection.

items.explanation: The ICC (1887) created ongoing federal supervision of railroad rates in the public interest -- the first great instance of Washington regulating private business as a referee. The 1906 meat act extended the same method to food safety. The Homestead Act gave away land, the Exclusion Act barred immigrants, and the Sherman Act attacked combinations rather than supervising an industry day to day.
options: A. The creation of the Interstate Commerce Commission (1887) to regulate railroads
B. The Homestead Act's distribution of western land
C. The Chinese Exclusion Act's ban on immigration
D. The Sherman Antitrust Act's dissolution of Standard Oil
items.stem: Which earlier federal action most closely resembled the Meat Inspection Act's approach?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the purposes hereinbefore set forth the Secretary shall cause to be made, by inspectors appointed for that purpose, an examination and inspection of all cattle, sheep, swine, and goats before they shall be allowed to enter into any slaughtering, packing, or canning establishment..."
—Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. The ICC (1887) created ongoing federal supervision of railroad rates in the public interest — the first great instance of Washington regulating private business as a standing referee. The 1906 meat act extended the same method to food safety.
option_explanations.B: The Homestead Act distributed western land to settlers — a giveaway program, not a regulatory system. It supervised nothing; it handed land out.
option_explanations.C: The Chinese Exclusion Act banned immigration — a prohibition, not ongoing supervision of an industry. Its method was exclusion, not regulation.
option_explanations.D: The Sherman Antitrust Act attacked combinations through lawsuits — it broke up trusts rather than supervising an industry day to day. The meat act's method was continuous inspection, not courtroom dissolution.

items.explanation: The packers denounced inspection as costly federal meddling -- then discovered the 'Inspected and passed' stamp restored consumer confidence and became a marketing asset. Muckrakers, consumers, and physicians had demanded the law; the industry fought it.
options: A. Muckraking journalists who exposed the industry
B. Urban consumers demanding safe food
C. Physicians concerned about public health
D. The meatpacking companies, who called inspection costly interference
items.stem: The Meat Inspection Act faced its strongest opposition from
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the purposes hereinbefore set forth the Secretary shall cause to be made, by inspectors appointed for that purpose, an examination and inspection of all cattle, sheep, swine, and goats before they shall be allowed to enter into any slaughtering, packing, or canning establishment..."
—Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Muckraking journalists did not oppose the act — Upton Sinclair's The Jungle (1906) and other exposes created the public demand for it. They were its champions, not its opponents.
option_explanations.B: Urban consumers did not oppose the act — they demanded safe food and were the law's beneficiaries. Consumer pressure drove the reform.
option_explanations.C: Physicians did not oppose the act — they supported food safety as a public health measure. They were allies of reform, not opponents.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The meatpacking companies fought inspection as costly federal interference — then discovered the 'Inspected and passed' stamp restored consumer confidence and became a marketing asset. Muckrakers, consumers, and physicians had demanded the law; the industry opposed it.
